Power & utilities

Secure your line servitudes and water infrastructure from the air

A register of the structures inside each servitude and wayleave, measured to the line axis, with vegetation change, fire near the line and fresh digging near towers flagged between surveys. For new lines and cross-border interconnectors, a route baseline and a cut-off-date register; for bulk water pipelines and dams, the same register along the pipeline and inside the zones your engineers define. A person reviews every result before it reaches you.

Send us your line or pipeline route How the method works

The problem, in your words

Servitudes are long, and what grows in them costs money

A transmission line crosses hundreds of properties and a bulk water main runs for hundreds of kilometres. Structures, vegetation and third-party works inside the servitude turn into outages, safety clearances, compensation and delay, and they are found on the next patrol if they are found at all.

“Houses keep going up under our lines.”

A structure inside the servitude is a safety problem, a maintenance access problem and, if it has to move, a compensation and resettlement cost. The earlier it is known, the smaller the conversation.

“We have to control vegetation in the servitude.”

Clearing crews need to know which spans have regrown and where tall vegetation stands, rather than working the whole line on a fixed cycle.

“Servitude acquisition is delaying the new line.”

Each structure along a proposed alignment is a negotiation. Knowing how many each option affects, before the route is fixed, shortens the path to a registered servitude.

“Someone has been digging near the towers.”

Excavation and earthworks close to tower footings or buried cables are found late. Line teams need to know where to look.

“Our water servitude records have gaps.”

Bulk water pipelines run for long distances through growing towns. Records of what has been built over or beside them go out of date between surveys.

“What’s downstream of the dam, and how many households are there?”

Dam-safety and energy-access teams need a current structure list inside the zones they plan for, and honest household estimates for the villages they serve.

Who this is for

  • Servitude, wayleave, land and rights officers
  • Line maintenance and vegetation managers
  • Land-acquisition teams and route engineers on new lines
  • Bidders’ development and E&S leads
  • Water utilities’ servitude, dam-safety and GIS teams
  • Mini-grid developers and energy-access programme teams
  • Telecom network planners and wayleave managers
  • Asset-protection teams, as recipients of flagged areas

Transmission and distribution servitudes

A register of the structures inside each servitude

We measure each structure the review confirms to the line route you supply, in its local UTM zone, and place it in the bands you set: the full servitude width, the safety zone inside it, and a wider band to see pressure building before it reaches the line. Each line segment gets a table of structures and each 500 m stretch an encroachment-density rating, so maintenance and land teams can plan which spans to visit and which landowners to engage first. The rating is a count rule, not a safety assessment.

Around substations and depots the same work runs as an area survey: structures inside the site and in a ring around it. Between dated surveys, new and removed structures are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, new tracks into the servitude are mapped, and a trend of built-up land shows where settlement pressure on the line is growing.

Fresh excavation and earthworks visible at the surface near towers and along cable routes are flagged so field teams know where to check. Drone checks of flagged spans capture the detail, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires, and if you already fly your lines we run the same analysis on your own orthophotos.

What you receive

  • A servitude register for each line segment: ID, coordinates, distance to the axis, band
  • An encroachment-density table for each 500 m stretch
  • Structures around substations and depots
  • New and removed structures between dated surveys, with before-and-after views
  • A change notice after each scheduled re-survey
  • Settlement growth trends and new tracks
  • Fresh excavation near towers, flagged for checking
  • Drone checks of flagged spans, subject to permits

Vegetation and fire

Where the servitude has regrown, and where it has burnt

Vegetation that has been cleared or has regrown along the servitude is mapped between dates from Copernicus Sentinel data, so clearing crews can be sent to the spans that have changed. It shows larger patches of change, not individual trees, and cloud in the rainy season can delay results.

Where tall vegetation matters, drone elevation models show where it stands inside the servitude, with open canopy-height data giving wider context. This locates tall vegetation; it is not a measured clearance to conductors.

Fire hotspots detected by satellite near your lines are filtered to the buffer around them, checked and sent as notices, followed by maps of the burnt area. Fire notices are not an emergency or early-warning service.

What you receive

  • Maps of cleared and regrown vegetation for each segment, compared between dates
  • Tall vegetation inside the servitude, from drone elevation models where flown
  • Fire-hotspot notices near lines and sites, credited to NASA FIRMS
  • Burn-scar maps after fires

Vegetation, land cover & fire

Where vegetation has been cleared, has regrown or has burnt along servitudes, estates and concessions, compared between dates.

Read

Vegetation management programmes

For a vegetation-management programme, the same maps help plan the work and look back on it. They show which stretches have regrown since the last clearing cycle, where vegetation cover dropped between two dates, and, where drone surveys are flown, where tall vegetation stands inside the servitude. Clearing can then be scoped to the stretches that changed, and the next survey shows where the cover changed after the work. After a line is rebuilt or a servitude restored, revegetation of the restored strip is tracked between dates.

The maps show larger patches of change, not individual trees or small plots. They do not measure clearance to conductors or sign off a contractor’s work, and cloud in the rainy season can delay results.

  • Stretches that have regrown since the last clearing cycle
  • Where vegetation cover dropped between two dates
  • Tall vegetation inside the servitude, from drone elevation models where flown
  • Revegetation of restored servitudes, tracked between dates

New lines and servitude acquisition

Compare alignments by the structures they affect

For a new transmission line, a distribution extension or a connection line, we count the structures along each alternative alignment within the servitude width and any wider band you choose. Route engineers and land-acquisition teams can then weigh options on the land they would affect, alongside their engineering, environmental and cost criteria.

Each option can be screened for slope, drainage crossings and ground seen as water in past satellite records, and the imagery history of contested parcels shows roughly when things were built or cleared. Once the route is fixed, a dated baseline with reviewer categories and estimated households supports landowner engagement, servitude registration and, where needed, the resettlement census.

What you receive

  • Side-by-side structure counts for each alignment
  • Slope, drainage-crossing and flood-exposure screening
  • Imagery history of contested parcels
  • A dated baseline register with categories, once the route is fixed
  • Estimated households, with the assumptions stated

New lines and cross-border interconnectors

A route baseline for every segment, and a register for the cut-off date

A new transmission line or an interconnector between national grids is acquired segment by segment, often by different utilities under different laws. The land record needs a date, and the same rules from one end of the line to the other.

We produce one route baseline for the whole line: the structures the review confirms along the alignment, measured to its axis within the servitude width that applies in each country and a wider band, each dated to the imagery it was confirmed on. The utilities on each side of a border, and the lenders financing the line, can then read the same register, segment by segment.

When the servitude and the substation sites are fixed, a cut-off-date structure register records what stood inside them on the imagery dates around the cut-off, with coordinates, a stable ID for each structure and reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding or under construction. It supports the census and asset inventory under IFC Performance Standard 5 and the national rules for each segment; it does not set the cut-off date or decide eligibility. After the cut-off, re-surveys flag new structures, confirmed by a reviewer, so your land team can show which arrived later, and an evidence pack fixes each register with file fingerprints and an independent timestamp.

Around substations, converter stations and switching stations, the same work runs as an area survey: structures inside each site and in a ring around it. Estimated households, with the assumptions stated, help plan consultation along the route.

What you receive

  • A route baseline for the whole line, by country segment and band
  • A dated cut-off-date register for the servitude and substation sites
  • Reviewer categories for each structure
  • Structures inside and around substation sites
  • Re-surveys after the cut-off date, with new structures confirmed
  • An evidence pack that fixes each register
  • Estimated households, with the assumptions stated

While the line is built

Access roads, tower sites and camps, recorded between site visits

Building a line opens the land along it: access roads, tower-site platforms, stringing yards, camps and borrow pits. Dated drone orthophotos and elevation models compared side by side show where ground has been cut or filled between visits, and volumes of borrow pits and spoil are calculated from the elevation models. New tracks and access roads are mapped between dates, and heavy plant visible on each survey date is recorded as a snapshot of work on site, never as tracking.

Clearing inside and outside the servitude is compared between dates from Copernicus Sentinel data, and once the line is energised, revegetation of camps, access roads and the restored working areas is tracked between dates. Together these give the owner and its lenders’ advisers dated evidence of the works between site visits. The evidence supports audits and environmental and social reporting; it does not prove compliance, and it is not a certified survey or a quantity surveyor’s valuation.

Drone surveys are subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires. Where the contractor or the owner already flies the works, we run the same comparisons on that imagery.

What you receive

  • Cut-and-fill maps between drone visits
  • Borrow-pit and spoil volumes
  • New access tracks, mapped between dates
  • Clearing inside and outside the servitude, compared between dates
  • Heavy plant visible on each survey date
  • Revegetation of camps, access roads and restored working areas

Bulk water pipelines, dams and reservoirs

The same register, for water infrastructure

Bulk water pipelines run in servitudes just as power lines do, often through the fastest-growing parts of a city. We map the structures along each pipeline servitude, measured to the pipeline route, and flag new structures and earthworks between surveys. Around dams and reservoirs, structures inside the reservoir protection strip and in the zones your dam-safety engineers define are listed with their distance to the source.

Settlement growth and estimated households inside inundation zones support emergency-preparedness planning, flood-exposure screening adds context from past satellite water records, and the whole register can be refreshed on a schedule agreed with you.

Storms, fibre and towers

After the storm, and along fibre routes

After cyclones and floods

After a cyclone or flood, radar imagery maps the flooded area even under cloud, and a reviewer checks towers, lines and sites before and after the event on optical or drone imagery captured once the weather allows. It depends on imagery captured after the event, covers visible damage only and is not an emergency service. Pre-season flood-exposure screening shows which segments and sites sit in ground that has flooded before.

Terrain, flood & post-event mapping

Steep, erosion-prone and flood-exposed stretches highlighted, and before-and-after checks along your route after storms and floods.

Read

Fibre routes and tower sites

Telecom wayleaves carry the same questions. We map structures along fibre routes and around tower compounds, compare route options for new fibre by the structures they affect, flag fresh digging near buried routes so field teams know where to check, and check visible damage along routes and at sites after storms. In Mozambique, the Land Law’s 50 m partial protection strip applies to telecommunications conduits as well as power and water. Fibre routes, route patrols and planned-works checks have their own page: telecom fibre.

Mini-grid and electrification planning

Structure layers and estimated households for energy access

Mini-grid developers and electrification programmes need to know how many buildings a village has, how fast it is growing and what the land around a generation site looks like. We deliver a structure layer across candidate communities, estimated households derived from the structure counts with the assumptions stated in the report, and settlement growth trends that show which villages are expanding.

For generation sites, a land-cover baseline and the site’s imagery history show what the ground has been used for, and an area survey lists the structures inside the site boundary. Household figures are always estimates, never a census, and we make no claim that they meet any grant’s data requirements.

Mozambique, South Africa, Nigeria

Servitude widths and rules your register is measured against

Satellite-based surveys need no site visit and no drone flight, and are offered through our country sites across Africa. A summary of public rules for orientation, as of 26 September 2026, not legal advice; the sources are linked.

Instrument What it sets
Mozambique
Lei n.º 12/2022, de 11 de Julho (Lei de Electricidade), art. 43		 An administrative servitude of up to 50 m from the line axis, with a safety zone inside it, to be registered in the land cadastre and the property register; no compensation is owed to those who acquired their rights after the line was built (art. 43(10))
Mozambique
Lei n.º 19/97, de 1 de Outubro (Lei de Terras), art. 8		 A 50 m partial protection zone on each side of electricity, water and telecommunications conduits (8(g)) and a 250 m strip around dams and reservoirs (8(e))
Nigeria
NESIS Regulations 2015, s.3.1		 Rights of way of 50 m for 330 kV, 30 m for 132 kV and 11 m for 33 kV and 11 kV lines, divided equally either side of the centre line, with no structures under the line
South Africa
Registered servitudes and wayleaves		 Widths are set in each servitude; the Electrical Machinery Regulations (regulation 15) deal with clearances of power lines

Português · English

Mozambique

Electricity is regulated by ARENE. Because Lei n.º 12/2022 removes compensation for rights acquired after a line is built, a dated record of what stood in the servitude, and when, is worth keeping. The cyclone season makes pre-season and post-event checks relevant, and reports can be delivered in Portuguese for land services and district government. Drone flights are regulated by IACM, and aerial surveys also need authorisation under Lei n.º 6/2024, including for handing the data to you.

English

South Africa

The national Transmission Development Plan names servitude acquisition among the causes of delay, and lines inside the strategic transmission corridors that meet the DFFE power-line standard (GN 2313) are excluded from environmental authorisation, which moves land baselines earlier. A 2026 FIG paper by a bulk-water author describes gaps in encroachment records along water servitudes. Many utilities fly their own drones, so analysis of your own imagery is often the start, and free satellite fire information is already available from the CSIR’s AFIS, so our fire notices are a filtered, reviewed add-on.

English

Nigeria

Transmission sits with TCN, distribution with the DisCos, regulation with NERC and technical standards with NEMSA. World Bank-financed energy-access programmes such as DARES drive mini-grid planning, where household estimates matter. Drone flights near high-tension lines need a special NCAA authorisation requested in advance under Nig.CARs Part 21, so satellite screening leads.

How it works

From line route to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the line or pipeline route and the widths that apply. We agree the bands, the dates, the imagery and the deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures and vegetation change are mapped along the whole line from dated imagery, open datasets or your own orthophotos.

  3. Check up close

    Drone surveys capture the spans that need detail, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every automatic result, then each structure is measured, banded and rated, and the files are delivered.

More detail on how it works, the methodology and how we work.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, cleared ground, fresh excavations and tracks along lines and pipelines
  • Measure each structure to the route you supply, within the widths you set
  • Map vegetation change and tall vegetation, and filter fire hotspots to your buffers
  • Estimate households from structure counts, with the assumptions stated

What we don’t do

  • Measure clearance to conductors, or inspect lines, joints or equipment
  • Detect vandalism, theft or tampering, or follow people or vehicles
  • Model dam breaks or floods, or run an emergency service
  • Decide whether a structure is authorised or what compensation is due

Frequently asked questions

Can you measure clearance to conductors?

No. We show where tall vegetation stands in the servitude, using drone elevation models where flown and open canopy-height data for wider context. It is not a measured clearance to conductors, and open canopy-height data is older in places, so drone surveys give the current picture.

Can you follow our servitude and safety-zone widths?

Yes. We measure from the line route you supply, using the widths in your standard or the applicable regulations, and report each structure’s distance to the line axis. A survey can report up to six widths at once.

Do you detect vandalism or cable theft?

No. We flag fresh excavation and works visible at the surface near towers and along the servitude, so your teams know where to check. What happened and why is for your teams and the authorities to establish.

We already fly drones along our lines. Can you work with that imagery?

Yes. We run structure, change and vegetation analysis on your own orthophotos and elevation models, and use dated satellite scenes to keep the record moving between your flights.

How do your fire notices work?

We filter satellite-detected fire hotspots from NASA FIRMS to the buffer around your lines and sites, check them and send notices, followed by burn-scar maps. It is not an emergency or early-warning service, and small, short-lived or cloud-covered fires can be missed.

Can you help before a new line is routed?

Yes. We compare structure counts along alternative alignments, screen slope, drainage crossings and flood exposure, and produce a dated baseline once the route is fixed.

Do you model dam breaks?

No. Your engineers supply the inundation zones; we list the structures inside them and show how settlement there changes.

Can you work on a cross-border interconnector?

Yes. We produce one route baseline for the whole line and measure each segment against the servitude width that applies in its country, so the utilities on each side and the lenders read the same register. A dated register of the structures in the servitude and substation sites supports each segment’s cut-off date and census.

Can you show where vegetation was cleared along our servitude?

We map where vegetation cover dropped or regrew between two dates along each segment, from Copernicus Sentinel data, and where tall vegetation stands where drone surveys are flown. That helps you scope and look back on a clearing programme. It shows larger patches, not individual trees, and it is not a clearance measurement or a sign-off of anyone’s work.

Can you estimate households for mini-grid sizing?

Yes, as estimates. We derive estimated households from structure counts, and the report states the assumptions, such as the persons-per-household figures used. It is not a census.

Send us your line or pipeline route

Tell us the servitude widths, the voltages or pipeline sizes and what the record is for, and we reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
